## Today's Agenda

- What a codebook is, and its six parts
- One complete codebook, built part by part from the Twitch chat example
- The mistake each part usually has
- The single-coder note and the memo
- What the Codebook and Qualitative Memo contains on October 30

## What Today Is

- Today is a demonstration, not a work session
    - You watch one complete codebook get built, one part at a time
    - Every part is shown as finished text you can copy the shape of
- The example is the shared Twitch chat corpus
    - Your own codebook uses the same six parts on your own material
- Your codebook is written at home, not in this room
    - It is due Friday, October 30

## The Codebook Is the Instrument

- The complete set of instructions for coding
    - Not paperwork assembled afterward
- Think of it as a recipe
    - It states every step and every exception
    - The same message, coded twice, gets the same value
- The heart of a content analysis (Neuendorf, 2017)

Its clarity is the strongest predictor of whether two coding passes agree.

## The Six Parts

- **Study overview:** the question, the material, and the time period
- **Unit of analysis:** what exactly one coded item is
- **Variables:** each defined twice, with a level, values, and edge-case rules
- **Decision rules:** what to do when a case will not sort
- **Examples:** two or three real cases per category
- **Single-coder note:** the limitation, the safeguards, and the counterfactual

These six parts are the six graded rows of the codebook. The memo is graded separately.

## Two Rules for Every Variable

::: {.define}
**Exhaustive:** every case can be given one of the variable's values, with no case left over. Example: an "unclassifiable" value catches any message the other values miss.
:::

::: {.define}
**Mutually exclusive:** every case fits exactly one value, never two. Example: a message cannot be coded both "directed at the streamer" and "broadcast to the room."
:::

## Keeping Both Rules

- An "unclassifiable" catch-all guarantees exhaustive coding
    - More than one case in ten landing there means the scheme is incomplete
- Overlap between two values destroys reliability
- **The fix for overlap:** sharper definitions, or a precedence rule

## Part 1, Study Overview

Three to four sentences. The finished text:

> This study asks who viewers address when they write in a live Twitch chat. The material
> is the chat log of one channel's streams. The period is the first two weeks of
> September 2026. Each message is coded for its target, its length, whether it uses an
> emote, and whether it asks a question.

**The usual mistake:** the overview names the topic but not the time period, so a reader
cannot say what is being coded or from when.

## Part 2, Unit of Analysis

One sentence, stated once. The finished text:

> The unit of analysis is one chat message: one sender, one message text, one timestamp.
> Every variable is coded on that one message and on nothing larger.

- "The chat" is not a unit of analysis
- "One stream" and "one hour" are units, but each gives very few cases
- A vague unit makes every later count vague

**The usual mistake:** the unit is one message, but a variable describes the whole stream.

## Part 3, Every Variable Has Five Elements

For each variable, in this order:

- **Conceptual definition:** what it is meant to capture, in the abstract
- **Operational definition:** exactly what the coder does to assign a value
- **Level of measurement:** nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio, matching the values
- **Coded values:** every one, with what it means, and a catch-all
- **Edge-case rules:** two per variable, each written as a rule

Four variables done properly is the assignment. A fifth earns nothing extra.

## Part 3, Variable 1

> **Message target.** *Conceptual:* the intended addressee of the message.
> *Operational:* the coder reads the message and assigns one value by the address cues
> it contains. *Level:* nominal. *Values:* **1 streamer** (an at-mention of the channel
> name, or a second-person reply to something the streamer said); **2 another viewer**
> (an at-mention of a non-streamer account, or a reply to a specific earlier message);
> **3 the room** (no specific addressee); **9 unclassifiable**.
> *Edge cases:* a message with two at-mentions is coded by the first; an emote with no
> words is coded 3.

## Part 3, Variables 2 and 3

> **Message length.** *Conceptual:* the verbal extent of the message. *Operational:*
> the number of characters in the message text, counting spaces and emote names.
> *Level:* ratio. *Values:* any whole number from 1 upward.
> *Edge cases:* a deleted message is left blank; a repeated message is counted each time.

> **Contains emote.** *Conceptual:* whether the message uses the channel's emote
> vocabulary. *Operational:* 1 if the message contains at least one emote name from
> the project's emote list, otherwise 0. *Level:* nominal. *Values:* 0 no, 1 yes.
> *Edge cases:* a misspelled emote name counts as 0; an emote inside a quoted message
> counts as 1.

## Part 3, Variable 4

> **Asks a question.** *Conceptual:* whether the message requests information from
> someone. *Operational:* 1 if the message ends with a question mark or opens with who,
> what, when, where, why, or how, otherwise 0. *Level:* nominal. *Values:* 0 no, 1 yes.
> *Edge cases:* a question mark used as an emote stands in for is coded 0; a message
> with a question and a statement is coded 1.

**The usual mistake in Part 3:** the conceptual and operational definitions say the
same thing, or ordered values are called nominal.

## Part 4, Decision Rules

Rules for the cases that do not sort themselves. The finished text:

- **Precedence:** if a message both names the streamer and names a viewer, code the one named first
- **Emote-only:** an emote with no words is coded 3 the room, unless it carries an at-mention
- **Copypasta:** a copied block is coded by its content like any other message
- **Non-English:** a message in another language is coded for target only when an at-mention settles it; otherwise 9
- **Bots:** a message from a known bot account is coded 9 and listed for possible exclusion

## Part 4, A Rule Is Not an Intention

- A rule names the case, then the single action
    - "An emote with no words is coded 3" is a rule
    - "Be careful with emotes" is an intention, and earns nothing
- Every hard case you mention anywhere in the codebook has a rule
- **Four to six rules** is the working range, at least two per variable

**The usual mistake:** one or two rules for the whole codebook, or a rule that restates a
definition instead of resolving a conflict.

## Part 5, Examples

Two or three real messages per value, copied from the material. The finished text for
message target:

- **1 streamer:** "@channelname that jump was clean" · "you should try the other route next time"
- **2 another viewer:** "@viewer22 same, I missed it too" · "replying to the mod: yes it works"
- **3 the room:** "LETS GO" · "anyone else lagging"
- **9 unclassifiable:** "ok but" · a single emote posted by a bot

Examples do double duty: a reference while coding, and a check when re-coding.

## Part 5, The Usual Mistake

- An invented example
    - A made-up message is the gap between Exemplary and Proficient
    - The example must come from your own material
- One example per value
    - One case shows what fits; two or three show where the edge is
- Examples for some values only
    - A rule without examples is hard to use for anyone who was not in your head

## Part 6, The Single-Coder Note

- Paragraph one: you are the only coder, said in those words
    - Every reliability claim is a claim about your own consistency
    - **Stability**, one coder twice, not agreement between two
    - A weaker claim than agreement, and named as one
- Paragraph two: at least three safeguards against your own drift
- Paragraph three: the second-coder counterfactual

Leaving the limitation out does not hide it. Naming it is part of the grade.

## Four Safeguards to Choose From

Name at least three you are actually using, each described as what you do.

1. **Inclusion and exclusion rules** for every value, written before coding begins
2. **A frozen codebook**, with every later change logged by date and reason
3. **An ambiguous-case memo**, settled against the written rule rather than by feel
4. **A fixed coding order**, with sender names hidden wherever that is possible

Each one is something a reader can check in your project.

## The Second-Coder Counterfactual

One paragraph describing the study you did not get to run.

1. **How many items** you would have double-coded
2. **What number** you would have reported, and from which statistic
3. **How you would have trained** the second coder and settled disagreements
4. **Which finding is most at risk** if the second coder had disagreed with you

The fourth part is the one that takes thought. It names where your own reading carries the
result.

## Part 6, The Finished Text

> I am the only coder on this study, so every reliability figure is a measure of my own
> consistency, not agreement between two people. I re-code ten percent of the messages
> after a week and report the agreement between my two passes.
>
> I wrote inclusion and exclusion rules for every value before coding, froze the codebook
> before the full pass, and keep an ambiguous-case memo settled against the written rules.
>
> With a second coder I would have double-coded 50 messages, trained the coder on 20
> practice messages, settled disagreements by the written rule, and reported
> Krippendorff's alpha. Message target is the finding most at risk, because it depends
> on reading address cues.

**The usual mistake:** describing a second coder as if one were part of the study.

## The Qualitative Memo

- **200 to 300 words** on the patterns you saw during immersion
- **Its one job:** explain why the codebook has the values it has
    - Each value traces back to something the memo describes seeing
    - A value you cannot trace back is a value you guessed
- **Source:** your field notes from Chapter 7, not the topic in general
- It becomes the qualitative half of your results

**The usual mistake:** a summary of the topic or the plan, with no patterns from your own
watching or reading.

## Your Unit of Analysis {.discuss}

On paper or in a file, for your own project:

- Write the unit of analysis in one sentence, following the Part 2 shape
- Name the one thing in your material a coder could point at
- Keep the sentence; it is the second row of the October 30 codebook

## Common Problems

- Values that overlap
    - Hesitating between two means they are not exclusive yet
- A latent variable with no observable criteria
    - A concept was written instead of a recipe
- **Six variables:** cut to four
    - Each one is a reliability check and a results paragraph
- A catch-all doing all the work
    - A third of the cases unclassifiable means the scheme is wrong
- Rules that restate the value
    - A rule resolves a conflict, it does not repeat a definition

- Tell a **unit of analysis** from a topic
- List the **five elements** every variable carries

- Say what the **single-coder note** and the **memo** each have to do
